message.content:
**Killing VS Code (code.exe) from the command line**

On Windows you can terminate the VS Code executable (`code.exe`) with the built‑in `taskkill` utility.  
Below are the most common ways to do it:

| What you want to do | Command | Explanation |
|---------------------|---------|-------------|
| **Terminate a single instance** | `taskkill /IM code.exe /F` | `/IM` specifies the image name (`code.exe`). `/F` forces termination. |
| **Terminate all instances and their children** | `taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T` | `/T` tells `taskkill` to also kill any child processes spawned by `code.exe`. |
| **Kill by PID (if you know the exact process ID)** | `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` | Replace `<pid>` with the numeric ID shown in Task Manager or `tasklist`. |
| **List all running VS Code processes before killing** | `tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq code.exe"` | Shows the PIDs so you can decide which one(s) to kill. |

### Quick one‑liner

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F
```

This will close all running VS Code windows immediately.

### Using PowerShell (alternative)

If you prefer PowerShell, you can achieve the same with:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Name code -Force
```

or, to include child processes:

```powershell
Get-Process code -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
```

### Things to keep in mind

1. **Administrative rights** – If VS Code was launched with elevated privileges (Run as Administrator), you may need to run your command prompt or PowerShell session as administrator to see and kill those processes.
2. **Unsaved work** – `taskkill /F` forces the process to exit without prompting. Any unsaved changes in open editors will be lost.
3. **Multiple instances** – VS Code can spawn several helper processes (`code.exe`, `code-helper.exe`, etc.). Using `/T` ensures all related child processes are terminated as well.

---

#### Example usage

```cmd
:: Show all VS Code processes
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq code.exe"

:: Kill them all
taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T
```

That’s all there is to it!
